questions.q: What is the purpose of transcoding in a video pipeline?
options: Producing multiple bitrates, resolutions, and codecs from one source upload
Encrypting the uploaded master file so only the CDN can ever read it
Splitting audio from video for separate storage tiers
Compressing the file once into the single best format
questions.explanation: Devices and networks vary enormously, so one master is fanned out into a ladder of renditions and codecs that players can choose from. No single format serves a 4K TV and a 3G phone well.

questions.q: In HLS/DASH, what does the client actually download during playback?
options: One continuous file streamed over a persistent socket
Raw frames pushed by the server as they are decoded
A single progressive MP4 fetched with range requests
Short media segments listed in a manifest/playlist
questions.explanation: Both protocols are ordinary HTTP: the player reads a manifest and pulls a sequence of small segment files, which is what makes CDN caching and mid-stream quality switching possible.

questions.q: What does adaptive bitrate (ABR) mean?
options: The origin server drops video frames whenever the network path becomes congested
The encoder raises quality for scenes with more motion
The player switches between quality renditions based on measured conditions
The CDN compresses segments further for slow clients
questions.explanation: The client measures throughput and buffer level and picks the next segment's rendition accordingly, so the adaptation decision lives in the player, not the server or CDN.

questions.q: Why do CDNs matter so much for video delivery?
options: They transcode on the fly, saving origin compute
Segments cache near viewers, cutting latency and origin egress massively
They enforce DRM licenses at the network layer
They automatically convert HTTP traffic into faster UDP streams by default
questions.explanation: Segments are immutable and shared by many viewers, so one edge copy serves thousands of requests, taking well over 95% of the bytes off the origin and shortening the network path.

questions.q: What information does a master manifest carry?
options: Frame-level checksums for every segment in the stream
The DRM license keys for each quality level
Viewer entitlements and per-user session tokens
The available renditions (bitrate, resolution, codec) and where to find their playlists
questions.explanation: The master manifest is the menu of renditions with their attributes and the URL of each variant playlist, letting the player choose a stream before fetching any media.

questions.q: Why are videos stored as short segments (2-6 seconds) rather than whole files?
options: Segments are required by H.264 and H.265 encoders
Segments enable mid-stream quality switches, caching, and seeking
Filesystems cannot store files larger than a few gigabytes
Segmenting reduces total storage cost by deduplicating repeated scenes
questions.explanation: Segment boundaries start on keyframes, so the player can swap rendition or jump position at any boundary, and each small immutable file caches cleanly at the edge.

questions.q: Where does the original uploaded master file typically live?
options: In object storage, with transcoded renditions written alongside
On the CDN edge nodes closest to the uploader
In a relational database as a binary column
On the transcoding worker's local disk for the video's whole lifetime
questions.explanation: Object storage gives durable, cheap, effectively unbounded capacity and is readable by any worker, so the master is kept there for re-encoding when new codecs or ladders arrive.

questions.q: Which stage is the most compute-intensive in the upload pipeline?
options: Generating the preview thumbnail images shown in the player
Writing metadata rows for search indexing
Encoding the source into the ladder of renditions
Virus-scanning the uploaded container file
questions.explanation: Encoding runs motion estimation over every frame and repeats that for each rung of the ladder, dwarfing thumbnailing or metadata writes and often needing a whole fleet of workers.

questions.q: Playback starts fast but stalls repeatedly on mobile networks. Which player-side factor most directly governs the stall/quality tradeoff?
options: The TLS version negotiated with the edge server
Buffer size and the aggressiveness of the ABR algorithm
The codec profile chosen at upload time
Whether the manifest lists its renditions in ascending bitrate order
questions.explanation: A deeper buffer plus a more conservative ABR ladder-climb absorbs bandwidth dips and prevents rebuffering, at the cost of slower startup and occasionally lower quality.

questions.q: A 2-hour movie upload must be transcoded quickly. How do pipelines parallelize this?
options: Split the source into chunks, transcode in parallel, stitch and align segments
Encode the renditions sequentially from lowest quality to highest
Ship the whole file to the fastest single GPU available
Transcode only the first ten minutes before publishing
questions.explanation: Chunked (distributed) encoding splits at keyframe boundaries so hundreds of workers encode in parallel, then the outputs are concatenated with aligned GOPs so renditions stay switchable.

questions.q: Live streaming differs from VOD most fundamentally in that:
options: Live streams cannot use CDNs because their content is never cacheable
Live video entirely skips transcoding to save time
VOD requires manifests while live playback does not
Segments are produced continuously, and the manifest updates as new ones appear
questions.explanation: In live the media is generated as it happens, so the playlist is a rolling window the player must re-fetch, whereas a VOD manifest is complete and static from the start.

questions.q: Viewers complain live latency is 30+ seconds behind. Which lever reduces glass-to-glass latency most directly?
options: Adding additional CDN regions between the origin and every viewer region
Raising the video bitrate so buffers fill faster
Shorter segments (or chunked LL-HLS transfer) and smaller player buffers
Moving transcoding from GPU to CPU instances
questions.explanation: Most live delay is segment duration multiplied by the player's buffered segment count, so shrinking both, or streaming partial chunks as they encode, attacks the dominant term.

questions.q: A new episode drops and millions request segment 1 simultaneously; the origin gets hammered despite a CDN. Which mechanism prevents this?
options: Client-side retry with exponential backoff on every failed segment request
Encrypting segments so requests spread across keys
Increasing manifest TTLs to one hour at the edge
Request coalescing and an origin shield so the CDN fetches each segment once
questions.explanation: Coalescing collapses concurrent misses for the same key into one upstream fetch, and a mid-tier shield funnels all edges through a single origin request instead of thousands.

questions.q: Why does per-title (content-aware) encoding save bandwidth versus a fixed ladder?
options: It reuses segments across titles that share footage
It caps every title at 1080p, cutting bitrate uniformly
Simple content reaches target quality at lower bitrates, so ladders adapt per title
It shifts encoding cost to the client's hardware decoder
questions.explanation: A static cartoon needs far fewer bits than a snowy action scene for the same perceptual quality, so choosing rungs from each title's own quality-versus-bitrate curve cuts bytes with no visible loss.

questions.q: DRM-protected playback requires which flow before video decrypts?
options: The player obtains a content key from a license server after device attestation
The CDN edge node decrypts each segment after validating the viewer's session cookie
The manifest embeds decryption keys readable only over TLS
The OS validates a watermark burned into each frame
questions.explanation: The content decryption module proves the device's identity and security level to a license server, which returns a key bound to that device, so segments stay encrypted end to end including on the CDN.

questions.q: Thumbnails, manifests, and segments have very different traffic patterns. Which caching statement is right?
options: Segments must never be cached because they are copyrighted
Immutable segments can cache long; live manifests need short TTLs
Manifests should be cached the longest because they are requested most often
Thumbnails should bypass the CDN to keep them fresh
questions.explanation: TTL should follow mutability: a published segment never changes and can cache for a year, while a live playlist changes every segment and must expire in seconds.

questions.q: Capacity: 10k concurrent viewers on a 5 Mbps rendition with 95% CDN offload. Roughly what origin egress remains?
options: About 50 Gbps served from origin
About 250 Mbps served from origin
About 2.5 Gbps served from origin
About 25 Mbps served from origin
questions.explanation: Total demand is 10,000 times 5 Mbps, or 50 Gbps; the origin serves the 5% the CDN misses, which is 2.5 Gbps.

questions.q: A global live event will hit 5M concurrent viewers. Which origin/CDN architecture handles the manifest update load?
options: Every viewer polls the origin directly for manifest updates to guarantee freshness
Tiered CDN with origin shield; edges serve manifests with second-level TTLs
Per-viewer personalized manifests generated at the origin
Pushing manifests to viewers over per-user WebSocket channels
questions.explanation: Even a one-second TTL collapses millions of identical manifest polls into one origin fetch per second per edge, and the shield tier reduces that further. Personalizing manifests would make them uncacheable.

questions.q: Storage math: a 1-hour video, ladder totaling 25 Mbps across all renditions. Approximate storage per video before replication?
options: Roughly 11 GB
Roughly 1.1 GB
Roughly 110 GB
Roughly 110 MB
questions.explanation: 25 Mbps times 3,600 seconds is 90,000 megabits, and dividing by 8 gives about 11,250 MB, roughly 11 GB.

questions.q: Post-mortem: a bad encoder build produced corrupt mid-quality segments; players kept switching into them and failing. Which safeguard best prevents recurrence?
options: Players permanently blacklisting any rendition after a single segment error
Manual spot checks of one segment per title before publish
Retrying corrupt segments at the CDN until checksums pass
Automated per-rendition validation (decode checks) gating publication
questions.explanation: Decoding and quality-checking every rendition before it is published catches bad encoder output at the source. Retrying at the CDN cannot help when the stored bytes are themselves corrupt.
